📖 The course

One essay. A complete writing practice.

A proposed two-week journey for people with ideas to express: an essay, a thoughtful recommendation, or a point of view. Work at your own pace. Each lesson combines an example, an exercise, and focused critique.

Days 1–3

📝 Find the point

Choose your reader. Name the question. Separate your claim from the observations supporting it.

You make: a thesis and argument map.
Days 4–7

🔎 Earn the conclusion

Find hidden assumptions, consider a strong objection, and revise without making your evidence sound stronger than it is.

You make: a first complete essay.
Days 8–11

🧭 Give it shape

Compare alternatives when relevant. Order your paragraphs around the reader’s questions. Replace vague language with precise meaning.

You make: a structured second draft.
Days 12–14

✍️ Make it yours

Edit with intention, finish your piece, and write on a new topic without help to see what carries over.

You make: a finished essay and a fresh attempt.

🧠 See the learning, not just the polish.

Know what changed.
Know what you can do next.

Keep your first attempt beside your revisions. Track the specific habits you are practicing. Then check them again on a new piece, without hints.

We’re designing feedback around clear criteria, not a mysterious “good writing” score. AI assessments are guidance, and may be wrong. You decide what to keep.

📚 A curriculum with a foundation.

Established ideas. Practical exercises.

Our existing five-phase engine informs the course. These methods guide the teaching; their combination is our design, not a scientifically validated scoring system.

  1. Map the argument: claim, evidence, and the bridge between them, inspired by Stephen Toulmin’s The Uses of Argument.
  2. Stress-test the idea: consider objections and possible failure, informed by Gary Klein’s Premortem Method.
  3. Question assumptions: distinguish confidence from support, informed by Kahneman and Tversky’s work on judgment under uncertainty.
  4. Frame the choice: compare alternatives when making a recommendation, informed by the reversible-decision distinction.
  5. Shape the draft: organize supporting ideas around a main point, inspired by Barbara Minto’s Pyramid Principle.

Will AI write my essay?

The course is designed to help you practice. AI points out weaknesses and guides revision; you write the work and decide which suggestions to accept.

Do I need an AI subscription?

The planned hosted course includes a stated feedback allowance. You won’t need to provide your own AI key or subscription.

Does this guarantee improvement?

No. Independent exercises are designed to help you observe progress. We have not yet validated learning outcomes for this course.

Can I enroll today?

Not yet. Explore the sample now. Paid access will open once delivery, billing, and support are ready.
